q: Fill up: The first stage of labour ends with ______, and the fourth stage is defined as the first ______ after delivery of the placenta.
opts: full cervical dilatation; hour
delivery of the baby; two hours
full cervical dilatation; two hours
delivery of the placenta; six hours
exp: The stages are: first to full dilatation, second to delivery of the baby, third to delivery of the placenta, and fourth the first hour of observation.

q: Which of the following statements about a prolonged latent phase is TRUE?
opts: It usually reflects an unfavourable cervix rather than obstruction, so rest and analgesia are the treatment
It is an immediate indication for caesarean section in every case
It is always caused by cephalopelvic disproportion or a contracted pelvis
It should be treated at once with high-dose oxytocin augmentation
exp: Therapeutic rest with analgesia lets an unripe cervix resolve; most women then enter the active phase or are not in true labour.

sec: Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
q: Fill up: In the active phase of the first stage, cervical dilatation normally proceeds at least at ______ cm per hour.
exp: A rate below about 1 cm per hour in a primigravida is protraction, which prompts a search for poor contractions, malposition or disproportion.

sec: Arrest of active phase & arrest of descent
q: A primigravida's partogram shows the cervix at 6 cm with no further change for four hours despite adequate contractions, and the head is at station zero. What is the diagnosis and next step?
opts: Arrest of the active phase — reassess for disproportion and deliver by caesarean section
Normal progress — continue to observe for another four hours
Prolonged latent phase — give sedatives and allow her to rest
Precipitate labour — prepare for immediate delivery
exp: No cervical change for four hours with adequate contractions, or two hours without, is arrest of dilatation and needs delivery after excluding disproportion.

q: Fill up: In a primigravida the second stage normally lasts up to ______ hours without epidural analgesia, and up to ______ hours with an epidural.
exp: Two hours (three with an epidural) is the accepted limit in a primigravida, and one hour (two with an epidural) in a multiparous woman.

q: All of the following are features of obstructed labour EXCEPT:
opts: A well-flexed deeply engaged head with no caput or moulding
A retraction ring rising obliquely across the abdomen
A tonically contracted tender uterus in an exhausted, dehydrated woman
A distended bladder, ketosis and a hot dry vagina
exp: Obstruction produces marked caput and moulding with non-engagement; a well-flexed engaged head with no caput is a favourable, unobstructed picture.

q: Match the ring with its description — 1) Physiological retraction ring 2) Bandl's ring 3) Constriction ring … A) A pathological ring that rises obliquely across the abdomen as obstructed labour advances B) The normal junction of active upper and passive lower segment that cannot be felt abdominally C) A localised spasm of uterine muscle around a fetal part, unrelated to the segmental junction
exp: The physiological ring is normal and impalpable, Bandl's ring is the rising sign of obstruction, and a constriction ring is a focal spasm.

sec: WHO recommendations for admission & first stage care
q: Which of the following is consistent with WHO recommendations for care in normal labour?
opts: A companion of the woman's choice, oral fluids, freedom of movement and no routine enema or shaving
A routine admission enema, pubic shaving and nil by mouth for every woman
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring for every woman in labour
Routine episiotomy and routine early amniotomy to shorten labour
exp: WHO supports respectful, low-intervention care; enemas, shaving, routine amniotomy and routine episiotomy are not recommended.

sec: Management of second stage & prevention of perineal tear
q: Fill up: Perineal trauma is reduced by applying ______ to the perineum in the second stage and by ______.
opts: warm compresses with hands-on support; avoiding routine episiotomy
a routine mediolateral episiotomy; fundal pressure
sustained Valsalva pushing; the lithotomy position
a routine episiotomy; early cord clamping
exp: Warm compresses, hands-on support and spontaneous pushing reduce tears; episiotomy and fundal pressure increase trauma.
